title: Modeling of Alkali Behavior with Cold Agglomerated Briquettes Charged in the Blast Furnace
abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing the steel production chain is essential for advancing toward more sustainable industrial practices. In ironmaking, agglomeration processes are significant sources of CO 2  emissions owing to their intensive use of fossil fuels. This study investigates the introduction of cold-agglomerated iron ore briquettes into the blast furnace as a low-emission alternative burden. However, a central aspect is the behavior of alkalis, which can form compounds (e.g., carbonates, cyanides, silicates) that may deteriorate the physical and metallurgical properties of the burden, degrade coke, and lead to solid build-ups on the furnace walls, reducing permeability and operational efficiency. A computational fluid dynamics (CFD) tool was used, and a new alkali recirculation implementation was integrated into the existing model, allowing analysis of mass transport, heat transfer, and chemical reactions associated with alkali cycling. The model was validated against reference operating conditions and showed good agreement, particularly regarding slag alkali concentrations. The simulation results indicated that the new briquetted burden does not significantly increase the formation of harmful alkali compounds in critical zones of the reactor. The study concludes that the use of cold-agglomerated briquettes is technically feasible and could contribute to reducing CO 2  emissions without compromising blast furnace operational stability. Measured and model predictions indicated that approximately 95% of the input alkali is eliminated by the slag phase for the four cases of industrial trials. Graphical Abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The steel industry ranks among the most environmentally impactful sectors, accounting for a substantial share of global carbon dioxide emissions, primarily owing to the heavy reliance on fossil fuels in iron ore reduction processes. According to the World Steel Association, in 2020, the production of one ton of steel resulted, on average, in the release of 1.891 tons of CO 2 , representing approximately 7–9% of total global emissions [ 1 ]. In response to growing demand for cleaner industrial practices, decarbonizing the steelmaking chain has become both strategic and imperative. This effort extends beyond energy source substitution, such as adopting green hydrogen, to include a reassessment of key process stages, particularly the preparation of the metallic burden [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ]. Sintering and pelletizing are the most established techniques for agglomerating iron ore fines; however, both are highly energy-intensive owing to their high-temperature requirements. As a lower-energy alternative, cold agglomeration processes have emerged as promising solutions, allowing the agglutination of fine iron ore particles with significantly reduced thermal input and a carbon footprint lower than pellets, lump ore, and sinter. Therefore, partial replacement of these burden materials is attractive for designing new cleaner operations with lower CO 2  equivalent emissions.

The technology under study employs sodium silicate-based binders, enabling the formation of briquettes that, after undergoing a low-temperature curing step, achieve the necessary physical, chemical, and metallurgical characteristics for application in blast furnaces (BFs). Their operational performance has been comparable to that of conventional high-grade burdens, such as pellets and sinter. However, the operational performance of the blast furnace could be affected if a large amount of alkali enters the burden materials [ 7 ,  8 ].

Figure  1  illustrates the alkali recirculation mechanism, which poses relevant operational challenges and demands careful consideration during briquette formulation. The incorporation of drying ovens following the compaction stage is a conventional practice aimed at improving mechanical strength and minimizing residual moisture. However, this thermal treatment is insufficient to mitigate the adverse effects associated with alkali contaminants [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13 ]. When the metallic burden contains alkaline elements such as sodium or potassium, particularly in the form of oxides, carbonates, or complex silicates, these species can enter a recirculating cycle within the reactor [ 10 ,  13 ]. At elevated temperatures, they tend to volatilize, then condense in cooler regions, only to react again as they return to hotter zones. This cyclic behavior may lead to the formation of scaffolds, localized corrosion, and reduced thermal efficiency throughout the operation, as schematically summarized in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Alkali recirculation and its influence on the formation of scaffolds in the furnace. (Schematic view constructed by the authors)

The main chemical reactions with the alkaline matters occurring within the blast furnace are depicted in Fig.  2 , together with a schematic representation of the furnace profile. The scheme shows the temperature distribution along the furnace height, while the reactions listed describe how alkali compounds are transformed under different thermal and chemical conditions. Particular emphasis should be given to the final reaction presented in Fig.  2 , where sodium silicates are reduced by carbon at very high temperatures. This reaction leads to the decomposition of silicates and the subsequent vaporization of alkalis, which then re-enter the recirculation loop illustrated in Fig.  1 . The combination of these mechanisms explains the continuous presence of alkalis in the system, reinforcing the challenge of controlling their accumulation and mitigating their negative effects [ 9 ,  12 ]. Fig. 2 Behavior of the alkaline compounds in the blast furnace and their main chemical reactions in different thermal zones. (Schematic view constructed by the authors)

The thermal stability of sodium silicate in CO-rich environments is represented in the Ellingham diagram [ 7 ]. Industrial blast furnace trials have confirmed its reduction behavior, with sodium being effectively removed through the slag phase. Based on Gibbs free energy calculations, the equilibrium temperature for the reaction of Na 2 SiO 3  with carbon was determined, as shown in Fig.  3  [ 9 ]. The results indicate that above 1550 °C, sodium silicate decomposition becomes thermodynamically favorable, releasing sodium vapor that re-enters the alkali circulation cycle, reinforcing its operational impact. At the same time, the equilibrium calculations highlight that even modest variations in the partial pressure of sodium vapor can shift the reaction onset, underlining the sensitivity of alkali release to local furnace conditions. Fig. 3 Relation between pressure of Na (atm.) and temperature (°C) [ 7 ,  9 ]

Given the inherent thermochemical and transport complexities of the blast furnace reduction process, computational modeling has become an essential tool for evaluating and optimizing processes within the steel industry. Techniques such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) enable high-resolution simulations of fluids, heat transfer, and chemical reactions, supporting the assessment of alternative metallic burdens and the anticipation of potential operational issues prior to industrial implementation [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 – 17 ]. This modeling approach not only reduces the need for costly experimental trials but also enhances process predictability and supports more informed decision-making, particularly in the context of the ongoing energy transition [ 14 ,  16 ,  18 ,  19 ].

This study focuses on the numerical modeling of alkali recirculation phenomena in the blast furnace, associated with the introduction of cold-agglomerated briquettes as an alternative metallic burden. The innovative approach in this research includes a dedicated implementation of new burden components, new chemical species, and rate equations coupled with the interphase mass, momentum, and energy within a CFD framework to simulate the transport, phase changes, and chemical interactions of alkali species under the thermochemical conditions of the reactor [ 18 ,  20 ,  21 ]. The objective was to characterize the behavior of these elements, particularly sodium and potassium, in terms of their reduction, reoxidation, volatilization, condensation, and reactivity within the furnace environment. In this investigation, it is expected that, with blast furnace operation using cold briquettes in the burden, under appropriate briquette formulations and reactor control, critical alkali recirculation patterns are not intensified and do not exceed critical values for scaffold formation or strong modifications of the incipient liquid formation. This modeling approach provides a predictive tool to evaluate the impact of burden composition on alkali dynamics, thereby supporting the safe implementation of alternative materials and broader efforts to reduce CO 2  emissions in ironmaking. In this investigation, four industrial trials of blast furnace operation were analyzed to adjust the kinetics of the alkaline compounds considered to occur within the furnace. Two trials, corresponding to actual operational practices, were charged without briquettes, and similar trials were charged with 6% and 12% of the metallic burden composed of briquettes. Afterward, additional hypothetical scenarios of conventional burden replacements by briquettes were analyzed.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: Since the last century, numerical simulation tools have undergone continuous development for analyzing blast furnace operations. In this study, a comprehensive multiphase and multicomponent model is presented, incorporating detailed physical and chemical interactions, as well as rate equations that dynamically couple the internal state variables of the blast furnace with the global kinetics of phase transformations and chemical reactions. The model integrates the thermophysical properties of each phase and chemical species at a local scale, allowing spatial and time resolution of the reactive system. The approach, illustrated in Fig.  3 , enables the coexistence of multiple phases within a representative control volume through volume fractions that express the distribution of materials in the bed. Each phase is characterized by its own set of chemical species and thermophysical properties, which evolve as the flow progresses through the reactor. These phases interact via interfacial phenomena, including momentum, mass, and enthalpy exchange, as well as through chemical reactions and phase transitions. The interaction framework is detailed in the multiphase coupling diagram (Fig.  4 b), which outlines the explicitly accounted-for exchange mechanisms in the model [ 17 ,  19 ,  21 ]. Fig. 4 A schematic representation of the internal state variables modeling is shown, employing a multiphase, multicomponent approach [ 16 ].  a  Illustration of a representative numerical control volume inside the furnace.  b  Mass, enthalpy, and momentum exchanges are involved in local multiphase interactions. (Schematic view constructed by the authors (Color figure online)

In Fig.  4 b, the solid lines linking two phases represent the complete set of interactions involving mass, energy, and momentum transfer. Meanwhile, the dotted lines illustrate that, beyond comprehensive mass exchange and chemical reaction mechanisms, the model also incorporates momentum-related interactions among the phases. The gas phase comprises not only the chemical species introduced via the blast but also those generated within the reactor through chemical reactions. The solid phase encompasses all granular materials introduced into the furnace through the burden charging system, including coke, lump ore, sinter, small sinter, pellets, and additives responsible for slag formation. Pulverized coal (PCI) is the material introduced into the furnace through the injection lances at the tuyeres. The liquid phase, represented by hot metal (HM), corresponds to the molten pig iron produced in the process. Slag is formed from liquid oxides generated during the melting process, including those resulting from the transfer of silicon, manganese, and phosphorus, as well as from additional chemical reactions involving alloying elements present in the pig iron [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]. The term “fines” denotes the small fragments generated from the disintegration of burden materials.

In Fig.  4 a, particle colors represent the different types of granular materials present within the reactor. In Fig.  4 b, the various phases and their complex interactions are illustrated through color coding: blue represents the discontinuous phases, while yellow indicates the continuous ones. Continuous lines represent the complete exchanges of momentum, energy, and chemical reactions. Dotted lines indicate chemical reactions and energy transfer between phases, along with limited momentum interactions [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ,  20 ,  36 ,  37 ,  39 ,  41 ].

To develop a comprehensive and interconnected dynamic kinetic model, local mechanisms of mass and energy exchange are incorporated into the formulation of the rate equations [ 19 ,  36 ,  39 ,  42 ]. This enables the model equations to account for variations in raw materials and diverse operational conditions. As a result, an extensive kinetic database covering a wide range of basic materials has been developed and integrated into the model framework. New fundamental kinetic data for chemical reactions have been continuously generated and incorporated into the model, drawing from experimental studies, industrial trials, and statistical methods [ 14 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 – 21 ,  29 ,  43 ,  44 ,  45 – 46 ], as the model is designed to operate using its own open-source computational code, which has been developed by the university in partnership with industry. The kinetic model principles were developed using a similar structural framework, but with distinct rate constants and parameters adjusted to reflect recent experimental findings obtained under controlled dimensionless conditions. Therefore, a computational code updated to account for the current scenario, characterized by a new metallic burden, is highly valuable for the process analysis. By applying this approach, it is possible to assess the impacts of introducing a new raw material source, with the goal of developing a green pig iron production route using the model built in the open computational simulation environment. It is also possible to determine the operational parameters that optimize efficiency and competitive performance, while reducing carbon dioxide emissions associated with the use of new raw materials. This approach also allows for identifying operational parameters that improve both efficiency and competitiveness, while minimizing the carbon dioxide emissions associated with the use of new raw materials. The present work incorporates new elements into the original computational code, including reactions among various chemical species and their corresponding rate equations.

The governing equations are formulated under the assumption of an infinitesimal control volume, as schematically illustrated in Fig.  4 a. The model assumes that conservation laws apply uniformly across the entire computational domain, which represents the actual operational volume of the blast furnace reactor. To accurately represent phase interactions, the model distinguishes between continuous and discontinuous phases. A set of balance equations, governing energy, momentum, and chemical species for the coexisting phases, is applied in accordance with conservation principles. These equations are presented in detail in Eqs. ( 1 – 8 ).

The phases and their corresponding chemical species considered in this study are summarized in Table  2 . The solid phase is divided into various components, each with unique chemical species and compositions, which undergo specific chemical reaction kinetics. To facilitate scaling of the modeling approach, the rate parameters derived from experimental studies are determined under conditions similar to those in the actual process. As a result, the core theoretical concepts can be applied to model all aspects of the process, as they align with the reactor conditions.

By incorporating operational data from process monitoring, the system of partial differential equations is solved under the assumption that the boundary conditions reflect those of a real blast furnace operating in steady-state. The incoming solid material is characterized by local mass consumption rates resulting from chemical reactions, melting, or gravitational forces. In contrast, the gas phase is treated as a fully developed flow governed by global conservation principles. The input of additional agents, such as oxygen, hydrogen, blast furnace gas, or pulverized coal, is quantified by their injection rates at the tuyeres.

The local volume fractions of the raw materials are calculated on the basis of the evolution of the burden composition within the furnace. These are determined by inlet boundary conditions, which account for solid consumption due to melting and chemical reactions. The progression of the descending burden structure is then computed in relation to the charging practice [ 14 ,  17 ,  20 ,  44 ,  46 ,  47 ].

The numerical solution of the transport equations is based on the finite volume method (FVM), which is implemented within a general non-orthogonal coordinate system to accurately represent the complex geometry of the physical domain [ 15 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ]. To accurately represent the blast furnace wall profile and the physical domain geometry, while preserving the advantages of a structured grid approach, the computational mesh is generated using a body-fitted coordinate system with locally applied smooth grid transitions [ 19 ,  50 ]. The semi-implicit method for pressure-linked equations (SIMPLE) is implemented within a staggered-grid framework, using covariant velocity projections to ensure consistent coupling between the mass and momentum conservation equations for continuous phases. Volume fraction conservation laws are applied to represent the behavior of the so-called discontinuous phases. The numerical coefficients of the discretized transport equations are evaluated using the established power-law scheme [ 15 ,  50 ].

A tridiagonal matrix algorithm is integrated into an iterative line-by-line solution strategy for the discretized algebraic system. This approach facilitates convergence in the three-dimensional domain, even in the presence of strongly nonlinear differential equations. It also supports iterative corrections related to cell volume estimates, phase interactions, thermophysical properties, reaction rate kinetics, and phase transformation mechanisms, while ensuring the inclusion of energy exchange processes [ 49 ,  50 ].

The phase volume fractions are computed iteratively by enforcing total mass conservation for each phase, while the momentum equations are used to couple the dynamics of the discontinuous phases. A power-law discretization scheme is applied to the momentum equations, and an upwind differencing scheme is used for the volume fractions. These are iteratively combined to obtain the numerical coefficients governing the solution of both the momentum and volume-fraction transport equations, on the basis of the mass balance for each phase. The numerical strategy applies to the power-law scheme across all phases and chemical species, allowing for the simultaneous convergence of the iterative solution procedure [ 15 ,  19 ,  48 ,  50 ].

The enthalpy conservation equations for each phase are formulated on the basis of the chemical reaction rate expressions, establishing a coupling between mass and energy transfer. A polynomial function is derived from the mixture rule to relate phase enthalpy and temperature, using the iteratively updated local composition. The specific heat capacities of individual species are locally evaluated under the additive assumption. Phase temperatures are then computed by solving the enthalpy–temperature polynomial using the secant method [ 19 ].

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs:
In this section, the simulation scenarios are analyzed to evaluate the behavior of alkalis within the blast furnace process. First, four reference cases, with and without briquettes, based on industrial operating trials, are presented, and their key operational parameters are compared to validate the model simulation. Second, a set of extrapolated scenarios is introduced in which pellets and sinter are progressively substituted, reaching up to 30% briquette participation in the metallic burden. Finally, a third set of scenarios is examined, considering the replacement of sinter and ore by briquettes, also up to 30% of the burden composition. The results of these scenarios are presented and discussed in the following subsections, highlighting the operational impacts and alkali circulation behavior associated with each case. sections.heading: Validation with Industrial Trials
paragraphs:
The model validation was carried out using four industrial trials with actual operational practice, designed to incorporate partial burden replacement with briquettes. These scenarios were tested in a small blast furnace with a working volume of 770 m 3 . Table  5  shows the burden proportions, solid coke, and pulverized coal injection for the four industrial runs used to validate the model for alkali predictions. As can be observed, the amount of pulverized coal, coke rate, and the proportions of pellets, sinter, and lump ore were considered to ensure proven long-term operational stability. In cases 3 and 4, briquettes were gradually added to the burden over 15 days of stable continuous operation (Fig.  4 ).
 Table 5 Scenarios for model validation Scenarios Coke (kg/t HM ) PCI (kg/t HM ) Briquette (%) Sinter (%) Pellets (%) Ore A (%) Ore B (%) Ore C (%) Ore D (%) Case 1 385.0 140.0 0.0 74.0 12.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 2 403.0 106.0 0.0 89.0 3.0 0.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 3 373.0 141.0 6.0 86.0 2.0 6.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 Case 4 383.0 150.0 12.0 85.0 3.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0

The validation of the model against industrial data demonstrated strong consistency, as shown in Table  6 . The main performance indicators such as productivity, coke rate, and slag rate were well reproduced, confirming the robustness of the simulation model, showing that the overall process behavior is in close agreement with the model predictions. The slag chemistry obtained from the model showed close agreement with the industrial reference, particularly for the major oxide components that govern mass and heat balance. A particularly relevant outcome is the excellent agreement between the predicted and measured alkali levels in the slag, which provides strong evidence of the robustness of the reaction schemes and the reliability of the thermodynamic formulations adopted in the model. Furthermore, operationally critical parameters such as basicity and slag viscosity were also reproduced with satisfactory precision, which reinforces the applicability of the model to process evaluation and scenario extrapolation. The high level of agreement achieved provides confidence that the model can be reliably employed to investigate the impact of alternative burden strategies on blast furnace operation. Furthermore, the model predicted spatial distributions of the variables such as phase velocities, temperature, and cohesive zone positioning. These patterns are useful for indicating stable operating practices confirmed for the four cases of industrial runs and predicted by the model. Figure  5  shows the inner distributions for gas temperature, solid flow and cohesive zone location, hot metal and slag dropping flows, and temperature distributions, respectively. The cohesive zone is clearly established at an intermediate height in the furnace, exhibiting a typical inverted V profile that ensures adequate permeability for ascending reducing gases.

sections.heading: Potassium and Sodium Inner Distributions Predictions for the Industrial Trials
paragraphs: In this section, we analyze the behavior of the solid flow moving with the alkali oxides due to charging practice and the transformations due to reduction, reoxidation, and complexation (to incorporate in the slag for potassium and sodium, respectively) for the cases with and without briquettes in the burden materials considered in the industrial runs. Figure  9  presents the distributions of potassium and sodium in the burden materials and the slag liquid phase formed. It is clearly observed that a central concentration of alkali compounds is due to the central coke charging practice. This behavior is expected to favor the alkali in the slag absorption and carrying gas. Similar patterns are predicted in Figs.  10 ,  11 , and  12 . Comparing the predictions for the industrial runs of these compounds. In these patterns, it is clearly observed that, as the proportion of briquettes in the burden is increased, the concentrations of the alkali compounds also increase, as expected. However, the concentrations are small. For these levels of concentration, it is not expected that significant changes in the initial liquidus temperature and coke reactivity will occur. The overall stable operation of these cases demonstrated that these operational practices can be established without loss of blast furnace performance. Fig. 9 Case 1: potassium and sodium distributions in the solid and slag phases with respective flow patterns Fig. 10 Case 2: potassium and sodium distributions in the solid and slag phases Fig. 11 Case 3: potassium and sodium distributions in the solid and slag phases for 6% of the briquette in the burden Fig. 12 Case 4: potassium and sodium distributions in the solid and slag phases

Figure  13  shows the predictions of precursor concentrations for scaffold compounds, comparing the four cases of industrial runs. It is confirmed that when the proportion of briquettes in the burden increases, the concentration increases. However, the maximum concentration did not exceed 0.15 ppm, which is negligibly small and unlikely to promote effective scaffold formation in the furnace shaft. Therefore, it is concluded that up to 12% of the briquette burden is feasible. The smooth operation of these industrial cases during a period of days supported this conclusion. Fig. 13 Model predictions comparison of the concentration behavior of the scaffold precursors in the industrial trials

sections.heading: Pellets and Sinter Substitutions
paragraphs:
In these extrapolation scenarios, simulations were carried out to investigate alternative operating conditions of the blast furnace, considering burden compositions, with briquette participation replacing pellet contribution and sinter. Three cases were defined in which the share of briquettes in the metallic charge was increased by 12%, 20%, and 30%, respectively, while the pellet fraction was simultaneously reduced to zero, maintaining the lump ore ratio; the additional replacement was sinter. These scenarios aim to evaluate the feasibility of the process and the potential impacts on gas flow, cohesive zone formation, and liquid-phase behavior under these alternative burden compositions. Table  7  presents the proportion ratios for these scenarios. In case 5, only the pellets were replaced by briquettes. In cases 6 and 7, the pellets were replaced within the initial 12%, and additional replacements were on the sinter ratio as the briquette increased to 20% and 30%, respectively. These cases were selected because of the possibility of raw material supply at the plant site.
 Table 7 Simulation scenarios with a higher participation of briquettes replacing pellets and sinter Scenarios Coke (kg/t HM ) PCI (kg/t HM ) Briquette (%) Sinter (%) Pellets (%) Ore A (%) Ore B (%) Ore C (%) Ore D (%) Reference 385.0 140.0 0.0 74.0 12.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 5 385.0 140.0 12.0 74.0 0.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 6 385.0 140.0 20.0 66.0 0.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 7 385.0 140.0 30.0 56.0 0.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0

To achieve briquette participation levels of 20% and 30% in the metallic burden, the substitution was not limited to pellet removal, since the reference case contained only 12% pellets. Therefore, additional fractions of sinter (89% in the reference case) were also proportionally reduced to accommodate the increase in briquette ratios. Fig.  14  and Fig.  15  present a comparison of the calculated results for cases 5, 6, and 7 with the reference case 1. Figure  14  shows the fusion region, as indicated by the fusion rate of the burden materials, confirming that no significant slag liquid formation is observed in the region of scaffold precursors, as depicted in Fig.  15 . Fig. 14 Comparison of solid flow and cohesive zone location for the replacement of pellets and sinter by briquettes Fig. 15 Comparison of scaffold precursor formation with the solid phase in the blast furnace for the analysis scenarios of pellet and sinter replacement by briquettes

sections.heading: Ore and Sinter Substitution
paragraphs:
In these final extrapolation scenarios, sinter was progressively replaced by briquettes at 20% and 30% of the metallic burden. In case 8, only the lump ore ratio was replaced by briquettes in reference case 1. Following this, the lump ore was maintained and sinter was progressively replaced by briquettes, up to 30%. The focus of these scenarios, as in the previous cases, remains on assessing briquette participation, particularly its influence on gas-flow stability, cohesive-zone formation, and liquid-phase behavior. Table  8  summarizes the participation ratios for each burden material in the analysis cases.
 Table 8 Simulation scenarios with a higher participation of briquettes replacing sinter Scenarios Coke (kg/t HM ) PCI (kg/t HM ) Briquette (%) Sinter (%) Pellets (%) Ore A (%) Ore B (%) Ore C (%) Ore D (%) Reference 385.0 140.0 0.0 74.0 12.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 8 385.0 140.0 14.0 74.0 12.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.0 Case 9 385.0 140.0 20.0 54.0 12.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0 Case 10 385.0 140.0 30.0 44.0 12.0 6.0 0.0 5.0 3.0

Figures  16  and  17  present comparisons of calculated results for cases 8, 9, and 10 for fusion rates and scaffold precursors. As in the previous cases, the fusion rates are significant in the lower part of the furnace, indicating cohesive zone stability, with negligible effects of scaffold formation, as evidenced by low liquidus temperature compounds. Figure  17  shows that a small concentration of low-liquidus-temperature compounds is formed (a maximum of 15 ppm). These predicted results indicate that these suggested scenarios are feasible industrially. sections.heading: Discussion on the Potassium and Sodium Compounds Balance in the Blast Furnace
paragraphs:
In this section, the predicted operational parameters for the extrapolation scenarios are summarized, and a detailed comparison of the sodium and potassium balances with the industrial trials is presented. Table  9  lists the calculated operational parameters. Detailed inputs and outputs of sodium and potassium for all cases, compared with industrial practices, are presented in Table  10 . As can be observed in Table  9 , productivity slightly increased compared with the reference case (case 1), while significant changes in the slag rate are observed owing to the replacement of sinter with the high iron content of the briquette. However, the slag basicity strongly decreased. As expected, the concentration of sodium and potassium in the slag increased as the briquette ratio in the burden increased.

In Table  10 , the specific potassium and sodium inputs and outputs are presented, referenced to hot metal production (kg/t HM ). Potassium input is mainly introduced in the process by the sinter and coke raw materials in the burden. Sodium, however, has the biggest contribution from the briquette. Nevertheless, both are mainly removed by the slag. As observed in Table  10 , around 95% of the sodium input from the raw materials is removed by the slag phase in all computed results, consistent with the measured values reported for cases 1–4, representing the industrial operation trials conducted in this study. Moreover, the total input of potassium and sodium compounds did not exceed 5 kg/t HM .

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The CFD-based model proved to accurately reproduce the main thermo-fluid and chemical phenomena in the blast furnace, with particular emphasis on alkali circulation. Validation against industrial data showed close agreement in productivity, coke rate, slag formation, and alkali content.

Following validation, the model was applied to predict extrapolated scenarios where briquette participation in the metallic burden was increased to 20% and 30%. These cases were designed through different substitution strategies involving pellets and sinter. In all scenarios, the furnace maintained stable operational behavior, with gas temperature profiles, cohesive zone geometry, and liquid-phase viscosities within the desirable industrial range. This result demonstrates that briquettes can be integrated into the burden without impairing permeability, reduction efficiency, or liquid phase stability. In all scenarios, the total input of potassium and sodium did not exceed 5 kg/t HM , and more than 95% of these alkali compounds were removed by the slag. The calculated internal patterns of temperature, solid flow, and scaffold precursors indicated that the blast furnace operation was stable across all scenarios investigated.

In cold-bonded agglomerates, production is associated with significantly lower CO 2  emissions compared with sintering or pelletizing routes. The findings, therefore, indicate that briquettes provide dual benefits: sustaining blast furnace stability while contributing to decarbonization strategies in ironmaking.
